newsitem.title: UK: Spring recovery seen for Euro oil refining margins.
newsitem.headline: Spring recovery seen for Euro oil refining margins.

text.p: European refining margins, which melted away some of their winter gains at the start of this year, were expected to remain steady and then edge higher into the second quarter, industry analysts and traders said on Thursday.
Milder weather, expectations for a light maintenance schedule and high shipping costs that have discouraged moving material to the U.S. will initially weigh on margins, particularly gasoline.
But stronger demand for products and a reduction in European refining capacity should then lift those values to above year-ago levels, they said.
"We're optimistic globally and especially for Europe across the full year," said Jeremy Hudson, head of European energy research at Salomon Brothers.

About 250,000 barrels per day of European refinery capacity will be shut in 1997, on top of growth in products demand that is outstripping a boost in global refinery utilisation of two percent, he said.

As a result, the gross refinery margin before fixed and variable costs for a European refiner will likely average $2.25 a barrel in the first quarter for Northwest Europe, versus $1.33 a year ago, and $1.75 in the Mediterranean, versus $1.52, he said.
For the second quarter, NWE margins should average $2.50 versus $2.11, and for the Med $2.00 versus $1.58, he said.
Heating oil prices soared in October in a race to replenish snug inventories in the U.S. and Europe ahead of winter, but then crude jumped toward its six-year highs to kick off 1997.
Peter Bogin, associate director at Cambridge Energy Research Associates in Paris, said he was not as optimistic for the first half of the year, especially with weak gasoline demand.
"We've had two months of relative feast and now two months of relative famine," he said, noting a drop in the net margin of about $1.50 in December from its November peak.
"After the refinery closures and refinery restructures...are felt in 1997, then we think we could have some improvement in refinery margins."
His first quarter European wide estimate for a net margin is $1 a barrel versus $1.50 a year ago, and about unchanged for the second quarter near $1.00.
"It looks like the first quarter is shaping up pretty well and could hold up versus a year ago," an industry source said.
Gasoline margins were seen fragile for the first quarter because high freight rates in Europe and a shut arbitrage may keep some barrels on this side of the Atlantic.
"I'm a bit bearish," on gasoline, said one Netherlands trader at a major oil company.
"Gasoline seems to be quite strong if you look historically at the crack and with the arb virtually closed, the States has to move up or Europe down."
"The message coming out is that the East Coast (U.S.) is already in a gasoline mode, and that's a funny situation for January that won't give structural strength to the gasoline market," he said.
He added that if the arb remained shut, those cargoes will find their way into the barge market, depressing prices.

The crack spread for prompt NWE regular unleaded gasoline against Brent crude is currently around $3.65 a barrel, and will likely fall toward $2.50, he said. The March spread is also at a lofty $4.50, he said.
"European demand will remain weak for gasoline in the first half," Bogin said.
But the industry source said the shipping conundrum will eventually sort itself out and the arbitrage invariably will open again -- both supporting gasoline prices and margins.
